laws.title: Code is Written for Humans First
laws.statement: Code is written for human readers first; any function must be understandable within 30 seconds, and comments explain WHY, never WHAT.
laws.rationale_summary: In a distributed team of 20–50 engineers, code is read tens of times for every time it is written.

laws.title: Quality is Built-In, Never Added Later
laws.statement: Quality is built in at the moment code is written, never deferred; a TODO without a tracked ticket and context is a defect.
laws.rationale_summary: Deferred quality is debt issued at predatory interest: unaddressed tech debt was one of the six founding pain points of this constitution.

laws.title: Consistency Enables Collaboration
laws.statement: All projects use identical tooling and conventions with zero project-level exceptions; conventions change only by amendment, for everyone.
laws.rationale_summary: Inconsistent standards across projects were a founding pain point: every project-specific convention is a tax on every engineer who moves between projects, and on every reviewer reading an unfamiliar repo.

laws.title: Architecture Decisions Are Intentional
laws.statement: System structure is the product of deliberate, recorded decisions; significant architectural choices require an ADR before merge.
laws.rationale_summary: Undocumented architecture is rediscovered at the worst possible time — by the next engineer, mid-incident, or during an audit.

laws.title: Security is Everybody's Responsibility
laws.statement: Security defects block merge regardless of author or deadline; only a named human security lead may override a CRITICAL finding, recorded in the PR.
laws.rationale_summary: Security vulnerabilities reaching production was a founding pain point of this constitution.

laws.title: Naming Conventions
laws.statement: Identifiers follow the constitution's naming table: camelCase variables/functions, PascalCase types without I-prefix, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants, is/has/can booleans, kebab-case files.
laws.rationale_summary: Names are the primary interface between code and reader.

laws.title: Formatting via Prettier
laws.statement: All code is formatted by Prettier with the shared config (2-space, 100-char, single quotes, semicolons, ES5 trailing commas); formatting is never manual.
laws.rationale_summary: Every minute spent formatting — or arguing about formatting in review — is waste, and review bottlenecks were a founding pain point.

laws.title: Prohibition of the any Type
laws.statement: The `any` type is prohibited. Use `unknown` with type narrowing.
laws.rationale_summary: any silently disables TypeScript's type checking for that value and everything it touches, defeating the purpose of strict mode and allowing type errors to reach production.

laws.title: Explicit Return Types on Exported Functions
laws.statement: Every exported function declares its return type explicitly; a public signature is a written contract, not an inference.
laws.rationale_summary: Inferred return types on public surfaces make the contract whatever the implementation happens to return: an internal refactor silently changes the API and the breakage surfaces in distant consumers, attributed to the wrong commit.

laws.title: Import Ordering
laws.statement: Imports are grouped stdlib → third-party → local, alphabetized within groups, enforced by ESLint — never maintained by hand.
laws.rationale_summary: A file's imports are its dependency manifest.

laws.title: Function Size and Responsibility
laws.statement: Functions do one thing, are at most 30 lines (target 10–15), and contain no magic numbers — meaningful literals are named constants.
laws.rationale_summary: Function size is the most reliable cheap proxy for responsibility creep: a 60-line function almost always interleaves concerns that must be understood — and tested (LAW-3.4) — together.

laws.title: Test-First Development
laws.statement: Tests are written before implementation; a failing test demonstrating expected behavior exists before the code that makes it pass.
laws.rationale_summary: A test written after the implementation tends to assert what the code does, not what it should do — it inherits the implementation's bugs as expectations.

laws.title: Coverage Floors
laws.statement: CI enforces coverage floors — 80% business logic, 100% utilities, 70% controllers — and they may not be lowered to make a build pass.
laws.rationale_summary: Low test coverage was a founding pain point: untested paths are where production incidents live.

laws.title: Test Structure
laws.statement: Tests follow Arrange-Act-Assert with one action per test, named 'should <expectation> when <scenario>'.
laws.rationale_summary: Tests are the executable specification of the system — they are read most often at the worst time: when they fail, in CI, by someone who didn't write them.

laws.title: Test Isolation
laws.statement: Unit tests mock all external dependencies, complete in under one second, and never depend on another test's execution or ordering.
laws.rationale_summary: Tests that touch real dependencies are slow, flaky, and ambiguous: a failure might mean broken code, a down service, or a dirty database, and engineers learn to re-run instead of investigate — at which point the suite's signal is dead.

laws.title: No Skipped or Hollow Tests
laws.statement: No .skip without a tracked ticket; every test must assert on behavior and be able to fail when that behavior breaks.
laws.rationale_summary: A skipped test is a known blind spot; without a ticket it is a permanent one that silently exempts a behavior from the safety net while still appearing in the suite.

laws.title: Layered Architecture
laws.statement: Applications use Presentation → Application → Domain → Persistence layering with dependencies pointing downward only; the domain layer imports no framework.
laws.rationale_summary: Layering is what keeps change local.

laws.title: SOLID Compliance
laws.statement: All modules comply with SOLID, verified by the one-line tests — one reason to change, open to extension, substitutable subtypes, lean interfaces, depend on abstractions.
laws.rationale_summary: SOLID is the difference between a system that absorbs change and one that shatters under it.

laws.title: No Circular Dependencies
laws.statement: Circular dependencies are prohibited at any distance; import/no-cycle is a build error, and shared concepts are extracted into a module beneath both.
laws.rationale_summary: A cycle means neither module can be understood, tested, loaded, or replaced without the other — they are one module wearing two names, and every module in the cycle inherits the union of all their reasons to change.

laws.title: Sanctioned Patterns
laws.statement: DI, Repository, Factory, and Strategy are required in their defined situations; novel patterns require an ADR explaining why the sanctioned set was insufficient.
laws.rationale_summary: A small sanctioned vocabulary means every engineer and agent reads every codebase fluently: a *Repository always means the same thing, in every project (LAW-1.3 applied to design).

laws.title: ADR Requirement
laws.statement: Significant structural decisions are recorded as an ADR in docs/adr/ before the implementing change merges.
laws.rationale_summary: The most expensive question in a legacy system is "can we change this?" — and it's expensive precisely because nobody recorded why it is the way it is.

laws.title: Universal Input Validation
laws.statement: All external data is validated at the boundary with allowlist validation before use; failing data is rejected, never sanitized into acceptability.
laws.rationale_summary: Nearly every injection class — SQL, XSS, command, path traversal, deserialization — begins as unvalidated external data reaching code that trusts it.

laws.title: Parameterized Queries Only
laws.statement: Queries are built exclusively with parameterized statements; concatenating or interpolating any runtime value into query text is prohibited.
laws.rationale_summary: SQL injection has been the most exploited vulnerability class for over two decades, and every instance begins with one engineer concatenating "just this one" value.

laws.title: Secrets Never in Code
laws.statement: Secrets never appear in code, committed config, images, or logs — runtime env/secret manager only; a committed secret is rotated, not removed.
laws.rationale_summary: Version control never forgets: a secret committed once survives in history through every clone, fork, and backup, beyond the reach of any later deletion.

laws.title: Established Auth Frameworks Only
laws.statement: Auth uses established frameworks (OAuth2/OIDC, vetted JWT, SAML) exclusively; custom cryptography, session, or token schemes are categorically prohibited.
laws.rationale_summary: Cryptographic and auth code fails silently: it works perfectly in every demo and falls only to an adversary — timing side channels, padding oracles, token confusion, session fixation — failure modes that don't appear in tests (so LAW-3.2 coverage cannot save you) and that took the field decades to discover.

laws.title: Dependency Hygiene
laws.statement: Dependencies are scanned weekly and per-PR; criticals are patched within 24 hours, lockfiles are committed, and versions are pinned exactly.
laws.rationale_summary: A modern Node.js application is mostly other people's code — typically hundreds of transitive packages, each a potential entry point.

laws.title: Encryption Standards
laws.statement: Data in transit uses TLS 1.2+ everywhere including internal traffic; sensitive data at rest is encrypted to current standards with managed keys.
laws.rationale_summary: Plaintext transport makes every network segment a wiretap point; "internal" networks stop being a defense the moment any single host, container, or VPC peering is compromised — which is why zero-trust practice encrypts everywhere, not just at the edge.

laws.title: Two-Approval Review
laws.statement: Every merge requires two approvals including one domain expert; authors never approve their own changes.
laws.rationale_summary: A single reviewer under deadline pressure converges on rubber-stamping; two reviewers with one required domain expert keep the review honest and catch the class of defects only context can see — a correct-looking change that violates a domain invariant.

laws.title: Quality Gates Are Inviolable
laws.statement: No change merges unless lint, type-check, tests, coverage, format, and security gates are all green; no override path exists for anyone.
laws.rationale_summary: A gate with an override path is a suggestion, and every suggestion loses to a deadline eventually.

laws.title: Public API Documentation
laws.statement: Every public function carries JSDoc with description, @param, @returns, @throws, and an @example for non-trivial surfaces.
laws.rationale_summary: A public function's signature says what types it takes; only its documentation says what it *means* — units, invariants, side effects, failure modes.

laws.title: Comments Explain WHY
laws.statement: Comments explain WHY — business rules, trade-offs, constraints — never WHAT; code needing a WHAT comment must be rewritten instead.
laws.rationale_summary: Code states WHAT perfectly and WHY not at all — intent, constraint, and context exist only in the author's head unless written down, and they are precisely what the next maintainer (or AI agent) needs before safely changing anything.

laws.title: Docs Travel With Code
laws.statement: Documentation is updated in the same PR as the change it describes; a behavior change leaving stale docs is incomplete and must not merge.
laws.rationale_summary: Documentation updated "later" is documentation updated never — the context evaporates the moment the PR merges and the author moves on.

laws.title: Human Accountability
laws.statement: A human engineer owns every merged line regardless of how it was produced; AI assists, humans approve, and 'the AI wrote it' is never a defense.
laws.rationale_summary: Accountability is what keeps quality real when generation becomes cheap.

laws.title: IP and Data Protection
laws.statement: No PII, secrets, payment/health data, client-confidential material, or proprietary algorithms may be sent to AI tools outside the approved list.
laws.rationale_summary: A prompt is an outbound data transfer: anything pasted into an AI tool leaves the organization's control and may be retained, logged, or used for training under terms we never reviewed.

laws.title: AI Audit Trail
laws.statement: AI involvement is disclosed at the point of record: [Claude-assisted] commit tag and the PR's AI Assistance section describing what was generated and what was verified.
laws.rationale_summary: Provenance enables every downstream safeguard.

laws.title: Identical Standards for AI Code
laws.statement: AI-generated code meets every constitutional standard with no relaxation; review verifies, never assumes — plausibility is not correctness.
laws.rationale_summary: AI output is optimized to look right — that is precisely what makes it dangerous to review casually.

laws.title: Mandatory Escalation on Uncertainty
laws.statement: On ambiguous requirements, lasting architectural choices, or unresolved security questions, agents stop and ask — guessing is prohibited even when the guess is correct.
laws.rationale_summary: Agents fail differently from humans: a human carrying an assumption mentions it at standup; an agent compiles it into the system, invisibly and at scale.

laws.title: Acceptance Criteria Before Implementation
laws.statement: No implementation begins without written acceptance criteria defining observable behaviors, in-scope edge cases, and verification.
laws.rationale_summary: Undefined "done" is how the same feature gets built three times: once as the engineer imagined it, once as the PM meant it, once as the client needed it.

laws.title: Business Rules Are Documented and Cited
laws.statement: Every implemented business rule cites its documented source at the implementation site and in its covering test.
laws.rationale_summary: Uncited domain logic becomes archaeology: five years later, nobody knows whether if (days > 90) writeOff() is a regulation, a client preference, or a bug that shipped — so nobody dares change it, and nobody can verify it's still correct.

laws.title: Regulatory Mapping
laws.statement: Regulated projects maintain a compliance map from each requirement to the code and controls satisfying it, updated in the same PR as changes to mapped paths.
laws.rationale_summary: Compliance that lives in engineers' heads fails exactly when tested — at audit time and at incident time, both of which demand evidence, not assurance.

laws.title: Scope Discipline
laws.statement: Changes outside agreed scope require explicit Product Owner sign-off before implementation; adjacent improvements are ticketed, not smuggled.
laws.rationale_summary: Scope creep is invisible until it isn't: each "small extra" seems free, but it widens the review surface (raising the odds defects hide in the unrequested parts), invalidates estimates, and ships behavior no stakeholder agreed to — which in client work can mean contractual exposure.

laws.title: Infrastructure as Code
laws.statement: All infrastructure is defined in version-controlled code and changed only through reviewed commits; console-clicked resources are prohibited.
laws.rationale_summary: Hand-built infrastructure is unreproducible by definition: when the region fails or the account must be rebuilt, the click sequence that created production exists nowhere.

laws.title: Deployment Safety
laws.statement: Every deployment is reversible with the rollback documented before release; a deploy without a rollback plan does not proceed.
laws.rationale_summary: Every deploy is a hypothesis; rollback is the safety net that makes shipping frequently rational.

laws.title: Cost Impact Assessment
laws.statement: Changes with material cost impact include a PR cost estimate and FinOps review; all cloud resources carry attribution tags; cost never overrides security.
laws.rationale_summary: Cloud spend is the rare cost that engineers commit in code and finance discovers on an invoice — a single misjudged instance class or unbounded log retention compounds silently at 730 hours a month.

laws.title: License Compliance
laws.statement: Every dependency license (including transitives) is evaluated before adoption; copyleft and source-available licenses require human legal sign-off.
laws.rationale_summary: A license is a contract accepted by npm install, and in client- delivery work the exposure is double: copyleft obligations can attach to the *client's* proprietary codebase, converting a free library into a legal incident and a contractual breach.
